item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Why the Mecca defence pact hasn’t triggered action against the Houthis
item.description:
Why the Mecca defence pact hasn’t triggered action against the Houthis

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have faced criticism almost immediately after signing the Mecca joint defence agreement last month, with questions raised about the newly formed alliance’s lack of response to Houthi attacks launched from Yemen against Saudi Arabia.

From the day after the signing ceremony, experts questioned whether Ankara would come to Riyadh’s aid as the Houthis targeted energy infrastructure and civilian areas in the kingdom.

The group’s takeover of stretches of Yemen’s coast near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait over the weekend, followed by attacks on the East-West Pipeline, which carries nearly 4 percent of the global oil supply, intensified the controversy.

However, judging the pact solely by the absence of an immediate joint military response overlooks several distinct questions: whether its defence obligations have entered into force, whether its members have built the mechanisms to implement them, and whether they are demonstrating sufficient political solidarity.

A senior Turkish official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Middle East Eye that criticism portraying the alliance as already failing was disingenuous and intended to belittle it.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Tuesday briefing: How to understand Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland’s joint call for change
item.description:
In today’s newsletter: Plaid Cymru, the SNP and Sinn Féin have signed an agreement for greater powers, as pressure grows on Westminster over the UK’s future

Good morning. Back in May, the shape of British politics shifted dramatically. I’ll forgive you if you were too preoccupied refreshing Andrew Sparrow’s live blog for the latest speculation about Keir Starmer to notice, but since 7 May, centre-left nationalist parties that ultimately aspire to leave the UK have been in government for the first time simultaneously in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

This week sees the initial codification of that shift. In Cardiff yesterday, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth, Scottish National party leader John Swinney and Sinn Féin vice-president Michelle O’Neill (who shares power with the Democratic Unionist party) affirmed their countries’ right to seek independence from the UK. Along with the leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald, they signed a memorandum of understanding that called on Westminster “to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland”. And they posed for a fair number of group photos too.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Exclusive: Mali’s Tuareg separatists seek Turkey talks, reveal Russian contact
item.description:
Exclusive: Mali’s Tuareg separatists seek Turkey talks, reveal Russian contact

Submitted by Levent Kemal on Mon, 09/14/2026 - 16:06
FLA spokesperson tells MEE that dialogue with the Africa Corps does not signal any rapprochement
An Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) soldier stands near a damaged Mi-24 helicopter at the former Africa Corps barracks at Camp 2 in Kidal on 11 May 2026 (AFP)
Off

The Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) in Mali has disclosed direct contacts with Russia’s Africa Corps and called for dialogue with Turkey to help find a political solution to the country’s crisis.

In an exclusive interview with Middle East Eye, FLA spokesperson Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane said the Tuareg separatist group hopes for engagement with Ankara, whose growing influence has made it an important player in the country.

Currently, the FLA is fighting the Malian government alongside Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an alliance of armed groups aligned with al-Qaeda.

While the two factions are coordinating their offensives, seizing towns and army bases, blockading Bamako and killing the Defence Minister Sadio Camara, they have different objectives: the FLA seeks an autonomous Tuareg state in Mali’s northeast while JNIM wants to topple the government.

Previously, French and other western troops propped up the Malian state against JNIM and its precursors.

But today, the government partners with Moscow, which deployed Wagner Group mercenaries in 2022, later reorganising them into Africa Corps units after Wagner’s mutiny against Vladimir Putin.

An FLA/JNIM offensive in April exposed the vulnerabilities of that Russian deployment in the north. Africa Corps personnel withdrew from the strategic city of Kidal before the FLA seized it. 

And in July, reports emerged of possible arrangements between the FLA and Africa Corps amid fighting around Anefis, 100km southeast of Kidal.

Ramadane said that the FLA have been in direct contact with the Africa Corps, but stressed that those exchanges did not amount to political negotiations or a strategic rapprochement.

“I can confirm that there were direct contacts in certain contexts, notably around questions related to movements, withdrawals and the situation in certain areas,” he said.

“In a conflict, there are sometimes channels of communication with the adversary to avoid incidents, manage certain situations or facilitate occasional arrangements,” he added.

“This does not mean that the political objectives of the parties have become compatible.”

A message to Erdogan

Ramadane insisted that northeastern Mali, the region the separatists want for an independent state they call Azawad, should not become an arena for a proxy war between foreign powers.

Yet, he added, that should not prevent the FLA from seeking engagement with Turkey, which has deepened its diplomatic, economic and military ties with Bamako over the past decade.

Ankara has sold armed drones and other equipment to Mali’s military government since 2023, while bilateral trade has tripled over the past decade.

Defence has become an increasingly important part of that relationship: since 2024, arms and ammunition have accounted for 20 percent of Turkey’s exports to Mali, ahead of electronic equipment, industrial machinery and cereals, according to a report by Le Monde.

Ramadane said those ties meant the FLA could not regard Ankara as standing entirely outside Mali’s conflict.

“We note that Turkey has considerably developed its relations with the criminal junta in Bamako, particularly in the sale of drones,” he said, alleging that the aircraft were causing civilian deaths in Azawad.

Nevertheless, he distinguished between Turkey’s relationship with Bamako and the role it could play in a political settlement.

“We do not ask Turkey to break its relations with the military junta. We ask it to look at the Malian reality in all its complexity and not to consider the question of Azawad solely through the prism of the authorities in Bamako,” he said.

The FLA wanted channels of dialogue through which it could explain its position directly to Ankara and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, he added, rather than via the Turkish military alone.

Ramadane said the FLA’s appeals to Erdogan were not an attempt to recruit another foreign patron.

“We do not ask Turkey to take a military side with the FLA. We ask it first to listen and understand,” he said.

He argued that Turkey’s influence in Africa and the Muslim world, combined with its close relationship with Bamako, gave it a particular responsibility.

“We do not ask Turkey to choose between Mali and Azawad. We ask it to contribute to ensuring that peace is not imposed on Azawad but negotiated with it,” Ramadane said.

“Our essential message is this: we are not seeking foreign patrons for our cause, we are seeking partners capable of contributing to a just, lasting political solution consistent with the aspirations of the populations concerned.”

A Turkish official familiar with African affairs told MEE that Ankara was open to dialogue with a range of actors and that channels could be found if the FLA wanted to engage with the Turkish government.

“However, it doesn’t mean that we will take their side and be part of the internal conflict of a foreign state,” the official said. “But we would listen to them.”

Battlefield cooperation with JNIM

Alongside its appeal for dialogue with Turkey, the FLA defended its battlefield coordination with al-Qaeda-linked JNIM, saying it did not amount to a political alliance.

Ramadane acknowledged that the groups had moved closer at an operational level against common enemies, but stressed that their political agendas remained fundamentally different.

“It is first necessary to distinguish two things that are often deliberately confused: operational convergence on the ground and political alliance,” he said.

In Mali, every foreign intervention failed - and jihadists adapted
Read More »

FLA and JNIM forces carried out coordinated attacks across northern and central Mali in April. A second coordinated offensive followed in July, including fighting around Anefis and attacks on military positions in Gao and Aguelhok.

Ramadane said the cooperation reflected battlefield realities rather than a shared political programme, insisting that any lasting settlement must address Azawad’s political status.

“The FLA remains an Azawadian political and military organisation whose project responds to the aspirations of the people of Azawad,” he said.

“That being said, lasting peace in Mali and Azawad will necessarily have to take into account the realities on the ground.”

He argued that JNIM, which he described as now composed largely of Malian nationals, could not simply be excluded from a future settlement.

“It is impossible to make peace in Mali or speak of stability without including JNIM,” he said, adding that the group was beginning to develop “a political language and an agenda of local demands”.

The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, says there is optimism that steel making will continue in his state, after the closure of a major blast furnace at Whyalla was announced yesterday.

Speaking to ABC News Breakfast from Whyalla and donned in some hi-vis, Malinauskas says there was disappointment, heartbreak, but also a sense of inevitability when the announcement was made.

[Whyalla] has the capacity to be a viable operation but it hasn’t been recapitalised. The blast furnace is over 60 years old. It was first built in 1965 and blast furnaces of this age not to be realigned on a frequent basis. This hasn’t been done in 20 years. The fact it’s still going is a miracle.

We need to have the plant recapitalised and that’s exactly the plan we have in conjunction with the federal government … if we lose this capacity behind me, this country doesn’t have structural steel-making capacity and we can’t afford that.

If Pauline Hanson wants to take us down the road of Americanising our politics, so people in a family who disagree on political issues can’t speak to each other any longer, this is the pathway to do it …

We’ve got lots of challenges facing Australia, but we’re not going to solve them by punching down on things that are brilliant about our country. So I think it’s rotten. I think it’s awful. I think it’s ugly.

I just don’t agree with those comments. But I actually do agree with Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price when she says that there are serious issues that do need to be discussed. And these comments shouldn’t be a distraction from them. I mean, why aren’t we closing the gap?
